note: Harness checks are direct safety evidence. Both route choice and queue instructions are plausible observations but weaker support. Feedback explains the distinction clearly.
An argument followed by an apology develops the relationship. Uniforms and classrooms establish setting instead. The short stem and feedback work at Bronze.

The priced meal and drink give the strongest evidence, but ¥25 alone does not establish good value for this audience. Supply the typical student budget or nearby price. Keep variety and convenience as competing benefits.
One control at a time shows how the game helps beginners learn. Later decoration and social scores are remote distractors. Ask what helps beginners learn and offer plausible tutorial features.
The map is a strong distractor for general navigation, but the next numbered room makes door arrows directly relevant. Feedback draws this distinction.
Hearing lyrics at the back shows clarity. Speaker positioning and applause cannot demonstrate it. Good simple synthesis of claim and exact evidence.

Correcting the sketch is individual teaching support. A greeting is individual but not teaching, and the group demonstration serves everybody. Specify help with learning and ask which detail shows the tutor helped one learner improve.

Testing the model demonstrates interaction. Photos and guide explanations do not require participation. Feedback adds that visitors “change” the model without that fact being supplied. Remove the addition.
Only B uses the finishing time with individual bus schedules. Ask how the listing helps readers get home and use plausible transport-oriented alternatives. Keep the walk as planning advice.

Five-minute service cannot establish that students can travel, eat and return in twenty minutes. The key overpromises and feedback addresses speed alone. State a four-minute walk each way or restrict the answer to the fifteen minutes left for travel and eating.

Instructions let visitors conduct experiments independently. The other options invent appearance or capacity benefits. The answer almost repeats the stem. Ask learners to distinguish independence from confidence or safety using specific instructions.

Only B follows from saving a completed level. Menus and score sharing are distant alternatives. Compare recommendations for different realistic journey lengths and limits on saving between checkpoints.

C gives the clearest specific effect for both facts. A adds an unsupported duration and a general reaction. B gives a reasonable verdict without explaining both impacts. Drop the invented afternoon duration and explain why an overall verdict alone does not fulfil this particular task.

The price and tools do not show sharing reduces practice time. The two balanced choices both make assumptions about the effect of sharing. Specify one pair and one bench per pair with only one person able to work at a time. Then ask how the trade-off affects beginners who want practice time.

Both A and C use realistic characters and slow pacing to advise different readers. The feedback rejects C for omitting a positive audience that the stem never requests. Set a reader preference and compare plausible choices as shown in the defect report.

B alone uses availability and free entry, but introduces sport when the source only mentions activities. A contradicts scarcity and C invents prices. Name the type of session and compare plausible differences in how early to arrive.

No choice can be validated without the end times and route to the bus. Feedback assumes the demo fits and that practical work cannot fit. Include both end times and the walking time, then distinguish attending in full from starting and leaving early.
